title: Platelets 92 and a cold foot
objective: Recognize heparin-induced thrombocytopenia from a falling platelet count on heparin, stop all heparin, anticipate a non-heparin anticoagulant, and flag the patient against future heparin
secondaryObjectives: Coagulopathies such as ITP, DIC and HIT, and managing bleeding and clotting disorders

brief.situation: 07:30 in a surgical ICU. You are Mr. Lindgren's nurse. He is 66, on day 6 after an open abdominal aortic repair, on a heparin infusion since day 1 for a deep vein thrombosis. Morning labs are back.
handover: Platelets: 240 on day 1, 198 on day 4, today's result just posted.
Heparin sources: the infusion, heparin flushes in his arterial line, and a heparin lock on an old central line port.

The night resident left a plan to 'start warfarin today for the DVT'. Unit policy for suspected HIT: stop every heparin source (infusions, flushes, locks) and call the intensivist; platelets are transfused only for bleeding.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the numbers mean and what has to stop and start.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Arterial thrombosis in the left leg progresses on heparin. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It still progresses with heparin stopped and no anticoagulant. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It barely progresses on a non-heparin anticoagulant. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Platelets transfused into active HIT: more thrombosis. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Warfarin started before platelet recovery: limb gangrene risk. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of an unsalvageable limb. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Every heparin source stopped within 5 minutes of the platelet result (unit practice).
The intensivist reviews and orders a non-heparin anticoagulant: about 5 min.
Vascular surgery evaluates and takes him for thrombectomy: about 25 min.

why.question: What do today's platelets and his foot mean, and what has to stop and start?

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: A platelet fall over 50% starting on day 5-6 of heparin, with new arterial thrombosis and no other cause, is a high 4Ts score: suspected HIT with thrombosis.
parts.modelAnswer: His platelets fell 62% starting around day 5 of heparin, he has a new clot in his left leg and there's no other cause. That's a high 4Ts score: suspected HIT with thrombosis.

parts.label: Stop and start
parts.criteria: Stops every heparin source (infusion, flushes, lock); calls the intensivist for a non-heparin anticoagulant at therapeutic intensity; no routine platelet transfusion; no warfarin until the platelets recover; vascular surgery for the limb.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop all heparin, the infusion, the flushes and the lock. Call the intensivist for a non-heparin anticoagulant and vascular surgery. No platelet transfusion, he isn't bleeding, and no warfarin until his platelets recover.

noProgress.rationale: Suspected HIT with a threatened limb still on heparin or without a plan an hour on is harm here.

expertPath.text: Platelets 92, down 62% from 240 on day 6 of heparin. Look at the legs: cold, mottled, pulseless left foot.
Stop the infusion; saline for the arterial flush; remove the heparin lock.
4Ts high. Call the intensivist: non-heparin anticoagulant, vascular surgery, cancel the warfarin.
Start the non-heparin anticoagulant; no platelets; enter a heparin alert; document every source stopped.

limbLoss.headline: Limb lost
limbLoss.body: A platelet fall over 50% on day 5-14 of heparin with a new clot is HIT until proved otherwise: stop every heparin source and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Platelets and warfarin make it worse.

salvaged.headline: Recognized and treated
salvaged.body: You scored the 4Ts, stopped every heparin source within minutes, got a non-heparin anticoagulant running and kept platelets and warfarin out. That is the expert path.

salvagedGaps.headline: To theater, with gaps
salvagedGaps.body: Check whether the flushes and lock kept giving heparin, how soon the anticoagulant started, and whether platelets or warfarin went in.

time_up.headline: No plan
time_up.body: Suspected HIT with thrombosis needs heparin out and an alternative anticoagulant within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A platelet fall of 62% starting on day 5-6 of heparin, with a new arterial thrombosis and no other cause, scores high on the 4Ts: suspected HIT with thrombosis. Every heparin source stops (the infusion, the flushes and the lock), the intensivist orders a non-heparin anticoagulant, and vascular surgery sees the limb. Platelets are not transfused routinely in HIT, and warfarin waits until the platelet count recovers.
